paras: The lynching of George Holden (George Bolden in the New York Age) was the shooting of a Black man by an armed mob that stopped a train west of Monroe, Louisiana, in late April 1919. Accused of writing an insulting note to a white woman, he was killed the day after nurses at a Monroe hospital turned back a masked mob that had come for him. The NAACP cited the case to Louisiana's governor before its National Conference on Lynching, and Black papers reprinted white Louisiana condemnation of the raid.

According to a Monroe letter in the New Orleans Times-Picayune, reprinted by the New York Age, Ouachita Parish had been "greatly aroused" by fourteen months of crimes and sensational events. Bolden had earlier been shot by a mob and left for dead, and one of his legs was amputated at St. Francis' Sanitarium. The letter stated that no charge had been preferred against him and that he was not under arrest.

On the night of Monday, April 28, a masked mob entered the sanitarium's colored ward and demanded Bolden from the two nurses on duty. Unable to identify him, the men seized a patient just out of surgery, who died of shock the following night. The police arrived half an hour late, left a pistol with a nurse and, by the nurses' account, told them not to resist if the mob returned.

When the mob came back within the hour, nurses from the white wards joined in holding it off; one fired a shot into the air, and another unmasked and seized a leader. The police, given the captured man, said he "escaped" on the way. Bolden was moved to the jail around midnight.

The next afternoon he was released to his wife, who put him on a stretcher in the baggage car of the westbound Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific train for a Shreveport hospital. Mob members aboard pulled the bell cord near Chemiere, about eight miles west of Monroe, threw him from the car and, joined by others waiting there, riddled his body with bullets. Shreveport wire reports added that two earlier attempts to lynch him had failed.

A coroner's inquest that afternoon found death at the hands of unknown parties. In a signed statement of May 1 the nurses wrote that it "certainly seems strange" that a man held by women escaped from officers. An Episcopal rector and a rabbi condemned the mob, Monroe's daily called for a special grand jury, and a federal inquiry was expected over the train holdup.

The Baltimore Afro-American reported resolutions by Monroe's First Baptist Church but noted the grand jury had not been called. The Chicago Defender said no investigation had been made, and no report of an arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Black Dispatch first carried the story on May 2 as a one-sentence wire item, "Mob Stops Train to Lynch Prisoner," stating as fact that Holden "wrote an insulting note to a white woman." The Chicago Defender's dispatch, dated May 9, ran as "Man Taken From Train on Stretcher and Lynched." On May 10 the Washington Bee and the Dallas Express printed the NAACP telegram to Governor R. G. Pleasant asking whether authorities had been "criminally negligent" and urging that the lynchers be tried.

The New York Age put the Monroe letter, the nurses' statement and the Picayune editorial "The Monroe Lynching" on its May 24 front page; the editorial likened the raid to German attacks on hospitals and said negligent officers "should be treated as members of the mob." Its own editorial, "A Southern Demand," treated the case as a Southern call for law enforcement. The Baltimore Afro-American praised the nurses: "What brave and determined women accomplished unaided, the authorities of Monroe could not do." The Cleveland Advocate noted the Picayune's denunciation on June 14.

Wire reports and the NAACP call the victim Holden; the Monroe letter and nurses call him Bolden. Shreveport dispatches called him a prisoner taken for safekeeping, whereas the more detailed Monroe letter said he was neither charged nor arrested and had been released to his wife. The wire placed the holdup about five miles from Monroe, the letter about eight.

reader.title: Lynching of George Holden
bases: An armed mob stopped a passenger train, took the wounded man from the baggage car and shot him to death after earlier attempts to seize him failed (A1, A2, A8).

An armed, partly masked mob with members on the train and others waiting by the track shot him to death without any legal process (A2, A6, A8); he was accused of writing an insulting note to a white woman (A1, A6).
Shreveport wire reports (A1, A2), the NAACP telegram (A5) and a separate Monroe letter reprinted from the Times-Picayune (A6, A8) agree that a mob took him from a train near Monroe and shot him.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire report
accounts.gist: A train was held up about five miles from Monroe and Holden, a prisoner being taken to Shreveport for safekeeping, was taken from the baggage car on a stretcher by an armed mob and shot after two earlier attempts failed.

accounts.label: NAACP telegram
accounts.gist: Restates the Shreveport dispatches and asks whether the authorities were criminally negligent in protecting their prisoner.

accounts.label: Monroe letter to the Times-Picayune
accounts.gist: Bolden, uncharged and not under arrest, survived a masked hospital raid on April 28 thanks to nurses, was released to his wife, and was taken from the westbound train near Chemiere and shot the next afternoon.

accounts.label: Nurses' statement
accounts.gist: The mob attacked the wrong patient, who died of shock; police came late, told them not to resist, and let a captured mob member escape.

framing.detail: Black Dispatch ran a one-sentence wire item, 'Mob Stops Train to Lynch Prisoner', stating that Holden 'wrote an insulting note'.
Chicago Defender headlined 'Man Taken From Train on Stretcher and Lynched' and noted that no investigation had been made.
Washington Bee and Dallas Express printed the NAACP telegram demanding prosecution, the Express under 'Two Lynchings Usher in the Nat'l Conference'.
New York Age gave front-page space to the Monroe letter, nurses' statement and Picayune editorial, and editorialized on 'A Southern Demand' for law enforcement.
Baltimore Afro-American mocked Monroe's protest at the 'lynching centre' label and praised the nurses over the authorities.
Cleveland Advocate brief relayed the Picayune's editorial denunciation.
